object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer entity in the system, identified by a unique account number. Represents the billing entity to which subscriptions are attached.

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.
account identified by account number

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A six-digit sequential identifier for an Account, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: The agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a specified billing cycle for a product. Identified by a subscription ID, prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a Subscription, generated with SUB prefix.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offered by the company. Identified by a product code. Currently three products: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: And products -- how are they identified? Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: A unique code identifying a Product. Current values: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artefact that specifies what a customer pays and how often. Identified by a plan code (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490). Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan? The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.
And I mean the billing artefact. The thing that generates the invoice line.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: A unique code identifying a PricePlan (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490).

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: The feature bundle or tier offered to customers, identified by name. Specifies the feature set, including number of seats, API access, SSO, etc. Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO. It's the thing on the pricing page.
What's the bundle identified by? Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: A unique name identifying a FeatureBundle (e.g., Starter, Professional, Enterprise).

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a plan change for a subscription, capturing the new price plan, effective date, and requester. Belongs to exactly one subscription.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record. We don't overwrite the plan on the subscription, we write a plan change with an effective date, and the subscription's current plan is derived from the change history... It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a PlanChange.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a Subscription begins. Always present and mandatory.

source_references.excerpt: Start date. End date, sometimes... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a Subscription ends. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front, that's usually an enterprise deal.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency at which a Subscription is billed. Must be either monthly or annual.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual... Only those two. There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current status of a Subscription. Must be exactly one of: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Every subscription in exactly one?

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a PlanChange takes effect.

source_references.excerpt: A plan change with an effective date... we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The entity or person who requested a PlanChange.

ambiguities.description: Plan ambiguity: The term 'plan' is used with three distinct meanings in the system. (1) PricePlan: The billing artefact specifying price and frequency (e.g., CORE-MO-49). (2) FeatureBundle: The feature bundle or product tier seen on the pricing page (e.g., Starter, Professional, Enterprise). (3) Sales plan: The negotiated deal structure used by the sales team, which may differ from both the price plan and feature bundle. The transcript does not clarify whether the sales plan is modeled separately or if it is a third system concept. The extracted model captures the first two as separate entity types, but the sales plan is noted as out-of-scope for this discussion.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan? The price plan... Tom: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle... Priya: And I mean the billing artefact... Facilitator: So we've got two things both called plan... Tom: We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither... Priya: Don't. That's a different meeting.

ambiguities.description: MRR storage and derivation: The transcript clarifies that Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) is derived from the price plan and billing period (e.g., annual plan of 490 yields MRR of 40.83) and is not stored as a field in the source system. It appears only in the reporting layer. However, the distinction between what is stored in the transactional database vs. the reporting data warehouse is not fully explicit. Confirm whether MRR should be excluded from the conceptual model entirely or tracked as a derived/calculated attribute.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR. Monthly recurring revenue... In the source system, is MRR a field somebody sets, or is it worked out? It's worked out... If they did we'd have a different set of problems... I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have.

ambiguities.description: Paused subscription status: Priya states that 'Paused' is not a status value, but a separate boolean flag that overlaps confusingly with the four official statuses (trialing, active, past due, cancelled). A paused subscription is still in 'active' status in the status field. The transcript does not clarify whether Paused should be modeled as (a) a fifth status value despite being called a flag, (b) a separate boolean attribute on Subscription, or (c) left out of the conceptual model as a system quirk. The current extraction models only the four official statuses and notes Paused as a known issue not in the model.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... Facilitator: I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly... Priya: Please don't. Finance reports off those four.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term cancellation and refund policy: When an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term, the system sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues with no automatic refund. However, there is no formal business policy: finance and sales disagree. Four refunds were given last quarter on a case-by-case basis outside the subscription system (manual credits). Whether the system behavior or the ad-hoc refund practice represents the true business rule remains undecided and is pending resolution by finance and legal. The conceptual model captures the system behavior (end date set to paid-through date, no refund field) but does not formalize the refund policy as a constraint.

source_references.excerpt: Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens? Nothing happens... Those were goodwill and they were signed off individually. Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down... cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues... the model will capture the system behaviour, which is that cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist.

ambiguities.description: Current plan field on Subscription: There is a discrepancy between how the subscription plan is stored. Sam initially corrected the facilitator, suggesting that a subscription does not belong to one price plan because plan changes exist. Priya then clarified that there IS a 'current plan' field on the subscription record (maintained by the change process, not set by hand) and that the change records represent historical data. The model captures this, but it would be valuable to confirm whether this current plan field is always consistent with the most recent plan change, and whether the facilitator's rule ('if the two disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug') should be formalized as a constraint.

source_references.excerpt: You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record... the subscription does carry a current price plan, and the change records are the history behind it... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Product roadmap and future products: Tom mentions that a fourth product is in discovery but does not yet exist in the system. The current ProductCode value constraint lists only CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT. Once the fourth product launches, the constraint will need to be updated. Confirm whether the model should include placeholder for future products or remain current-state only.

source_references.excerpt: Fixed at three? Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Account reuse and identity: When an account closes and the same company returns, they receive a new account number and are treated as a new customer for reporting purposes. However, Tom notes this 'drives me mad' from a product perspective because the company history is lost. There is an implicit tension between account identity (driven by finance's need to isolate revenue by account number) and customer identity (the underlying company). The conceptual model treats Account as the primary entity, but does not capture any link between the old and new accounts of the same company. Clarify whether a 'Company' entity should exist in the model, or whether account-to-account relationships should be modeled.

source_references.excerpt: never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... Tom: Which drives me mad, incidentally, because from a product perspective it's the same company and we lose the history... Priya: It drives finance the other way. If we reused numbers, revenue recognition would be a nightmare.

ambiguities.description: FeatureBundle price: The transcript establishes that a PricePlan entitles exactly one FeatureBundle, and that multiple price plans can entitle the same bundle (e.g., CORE-MO-49 and CORE-AN-490 both entitle Professional). However, the actual price or amount is not explicitly attached to either entity. Priya says the price plan 'says what the customer pays', but the extracted model does not include a Price or Amount attribute. Clarify whether Price should be modeled as an attribute of PricePlan, or if it is derived/stored elsewhere.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

ambiguities.description: Halloway incident and constraint enforcement: The Halloway Group example (lines 61) illustrates why the 'one active subscription per account per product' constraint is critical. Two different teams within the same account created duplicate subscriptions to the analytics product, resulting in double-billing for eight months. The constraint was added and is now 'enforced at the database level'. However, the transcript does not clarify whether 'active' means status='active' only, or whether 'active' includes paused and/or trialing subscriptions. Confirm the precise constraint: does 'one active subscription per account per product' filter by status value, or by some other definition of 'active'?

source_references.excerpt: A customer -- Halloway Group -- had someone in their finance team and someone in their engineering team both sign up for the analytics product, on the same account, three weeks apart... We billed them twice for eight months... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.description: Contact information and email: Priya states that company name and email are not on the Account; instead, 'Email is on the contact, not the account.' This suggests a Contact entity exists and has an email, but it is not mentioned further in the transcript. Clarify whether Contact should be modeled separately with a relationship to Account, or whether it is out of scope.

source_references.excerpt: Is there anything else that identifies an account? Email, company name? Company name absolutely not, we have four accounts called 'Acme.' Email is on the contact, not the account.

ambiguities.description: Plan change date discrepancy: The transcript mentions that a plan change record is created to track when changes are made ('who made it') vs. when they take effect, and gives an example: 'Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.' However, the model captures only EffectiveDate on the PlanChange. There is an implicit 'RequestDate' or 'DateMade' that is separate from EffectiveDate. Clarify whether the date a change is requested/made should be modeled as a separate attribute (e.g., RequestDate) or if the single EffectiveDate is sufficient.

source_references.excerpt: It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates. Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.
